The rain had been falling for hours.

Not the gentle kind of rain that helps you sleep. This was city rain. Cold. Heavy. Relentless. The kind that washed blood into the gutters and made the streets look almost clean from a distance.

I pulled into the parking lot of a small diner tucked between an old pawn shop and a boarded-up pharmacy. Neon lights flickered in the window, buzzing like they were barely hanging on.

The bell above the door jingled as I stepped inside.

Warmth hit me immediately.

Coffee. Bacon. Pie.

For a moment, it almost felt like a normal city.

"Honey, take any seat you want," the waitress called from behind the counter.

I nodded and slid into a booth beside the window.

Outside, rain hammered the pavement. Inside, jazz drifted softly from an old radio somewhere in the back.

The waitress walked over with a tired smile and a coffee pot in hand.

"What'll it be?"

"Coffee. Black."

She poured.

"You got any pie tonight?"

"Cherry and rhubarb."

"Rhubarb."

"Good choice."

She scribbled on her pad.

"How's the night treating you, detective?"

I looked out the window at the city lights reflecting off the wet pavement.

Truth was, it had been a rough one. Armed robberies. A gang fight downtown. Three hours chasing leads that went nowhere.

But I didn't feel much like talking.

The waitress waited for an answer.

I just took a sip of coffee.

She nodded like she understood anyway.

"Long as you stay safe, baby."

Then she walked away.

The pie arrived a few minutes later.

It was good. Better than good, actually.

For a little while, the world slowed down.

No sirens.

No criminals.

No dead ends.

Just coffee, pie, rain, and jazz.

The kind of moment a person doesn't realize they need until they finally get one.

Then the city remembered what it was.

The explosion rattled the windows.

Every customer in the diner froze.

A second later came another sound.

A roaring engine.

A very familiar roaring engine.

I looked through the rain-streaked glass just in time to see a flash of purple speeding through an intersection.

The Joker.

Behind him came a black blur wrapped in fire and thunder.

The Batmobile.

Someone turned up the radio.

"Ace Chemicals has reportedly been robbed," the announcer said. "Witnesses report the Joker was seen fleeing the scene moments before an explosion. Batman is currently in pursuit."

The entire diner rushed to the windows.

I stayed seated for another second and finished the last bite of pie.

Then I stood up.

The waitress looked over.

"Leaving already?"

I pulled a few bills from my pocket.

"Can you wrap the rest to go, Agnes?"

She smirked.

"Figured you'd say that."

A minute later she handed me a small white box tied with string.

"Try not to get yourself killed."

"No promises."

The rain hit me like a wall when I stepped outside.

In the distance I could hear engines screaming through the streets.

Batman.

The Joker.

And enough chaos to keep half the city awake until sunrise.

I climbed into my car, tossed the pie onto the passenger seat, and started the engine.

The tires spun against the wet pavement before finally catching.

I pulled out into the storm and headed toward the madness.

Because in this city, the coffee always gets cold.

The pie never gets finished.

And it's always another long night.

-----------------------------------------------------

 
Rain had always belonged to Gotham. 
 
It softened the city's sharp edges. 
 
Blurred the lights. 
 
Made old memories easier to mistake for ghosts. 
 
Bruce Wayne stood at the end of Gotham River Pier, his hands resting on the cold railing. 
 
The cape was gone. 
 
The cowl stayed at home more often now. 
 
His hair had become silver. 
 
His shoulders still carried themselves like Batman's. 
 
Some habits outlived strength. 
 
The river below moved lazily toward the bay. 
 
Bruce had come here to think. 
 
To remember. 
 
To wonder if Gotham would ever stop needing someone in a mask. 
 
A cane tapped softly against the wooden planks behind him. 
 
Tap. 
 
Tap. 
 
Tap. 
 
Bruce: "You're late." 
 
A familiar laugh drifted through the rain. 
 
Older. 
 
Rougher. 
 
Still unmistakable. 
 
Joker: "Traffic." 
 
Bruce finally looked over. 
 
The Joker wore an old purple overcoat. 
 
His green hair had thinned. 
 
The white makeup no longer hid the wrinkles beneath it. 
 
His smile... 
 
Somehow... 
 
Had survived the years. 
 
Joker: "You know..." 
 
"I always imagined our final meeting would involve explosions." 
 
Bruce: "You don't have the knees for explosions anymore." 
 
Joker burst into laughter. 
 
Joker: "Neither do you." 
 
Bruce almost smiled. 
 
Almost. 
 
The Joker leaned beside him against the railing. 
 
For a long while... 
 
Neither of them spoke. 
 
The city did enough talking. 
 
Sirens. 
 
Rain. 
 
Distant trains. 
 
Joker: "How's the family?" 
 
Bruce looked out across the water. 
 
Bruce: "They're alright." 
 
Joker tilted his head. 
 
Joker: "That's not what I asked." 
 
Bruce knew exactly what he meant. 
 
Dick. 
 
Jason. 
 
Tim. 
 
Damian. 
 
Barbara. 
 
The children who had become soldiers. 
 
The boys who had become men. 
 
The girl who had become stronger than all of them. 
 
Bruce took a slow breath. 
 
Bruce: "They left." 
 
Joker didn't interrupt. 
 
Bruce: "Not all at once." 
 
"One by one." 
 
"They built lives." 
 
"Families." 
 
"Careers." 
 
"They stopped waiting for me to become Bruce again." 
 
The words felt heavier spoken aloud. 
 
Bruce: "I kept choosing Batman." 
 
"Eventually..." 
 
"They stopped asking." 
 
The Joker stared at the river. 
 
Not mocking. 
 
Not smiling. 
 
Just listening. 
 
Joker: "...And Alfred?" 
 
Bruce closed his eyes. 
 
A long silence answered first. 
 
Bruce: "He died twelve years ago." 
 
Joker nodded. 
 
Joker: "I figured." 
 
"He was the only person who ever looked at me..." 
 
"...like I wasn't funny." 
 
Bruce smiled faintly. 
 
Bruce: "He wasn't easily impressed." 
 
Joker laughed softly. 
 
Joker: "No." 
 
"He wasn't." 
 
The rain grew steadier. 
 
Joker glanced sideways. 
 
Joker: "And the cat?" 
 
Bruce looked toward the skyline. 
 
Bruce: "Selina stayed longer than anyone." 
 
Another pause. 
 
Bruce: "She loved Bruce." 
 
"But Bruce kept disappearing." 
 
"So eventually..." 
 
"She left with the man she actually had." 
 
Joker frowned. 
 
Joker: "...Batman." 
 
Bruce nodded. 
 
Bruce: "That's the tragedy, isn't it?" 
 
"I spent my whole life protecting Gotham..." 
 
"...and forgot to protect the people who stayed." 
 
For once... 
 
The Joker had no joke. 
 
Only silence. 
 
After a while... 
 
Bruce finally looked at him. 
 
Bruce: "What about you?" 
 
Joker laughed. 
 
Joker: "What family?" 
 
Bruce shrugged. 
 
Bruce: "You always had followers." 
 
Joker waved dismissively. 
 
Joker: "They liked the act." 
 
"Nobody stays after the curtain falls." 
 
Bruce understood. 
 
More than either of them wanted to admit. 
 
The rain danced across the river. 
 
Bruce spoke again. 
 
Bruce: "Can I ask you something?" 
 
Joker grinned. 
 
Joker: "Oh good." 
 
"I was worried we'd spend the evening discussing our feelings." 
 
Bruce ignored him. 
 
Bruce: "When did you figure it out?" 
 
The Joker blinked. 
 
Bruce: "...That I was Batman." 
 
The smile returned. 
 
Slowly. 
 
Joker: "Earlier than you'd like." 
 
Bruce waited. 
 
Joker looked out over Gotham. 
 
Joker: "There was this night..." 
 
"You remember?" 
 
"The abandoned amusement park." 
 
Bruce did. 
 
Too well. 
 
Joker continued. 
 
Joker: "You'd just saved a little boy." 
 
"You thought nobody was watching." 
 
"You took off one glove..." 
 
"...and held his hand." 
 
Bruce frowned. 
 
Joker smiled. 
 
Joker: "Batman never comforted people." 
 
"Bruce Wayne did." 
 
Bruce said nothing. 
 
Joker chuckled. 
 
Joker: "I spent years trying to prove it." 
 
"Then one day..." 
 
"I realized proving it would ruin the joke." 
 
Bruce looked at him. 
 
Joker shrugged. 
 
Joker: "What fun is a punchline..." 
 
"...if you explain it?" 
 
Bruce let out a quiet breath that almost became a laugh. 
 
Almost. 
 
Joker pointed toward Bruce. 
 
Joker: "There it is." 
 
Bruce raised an eyebrow. 
 
Joker: "That little almost-smile." 
 
"I spent decades trying to earn one." 
 
Bruce shook his head. 
 
Bruce: "You caused billions in property damage." 
 
Joker nodded proudly. 
 
Joker: "And eventually..." 
 
"I got half a smile." 
 
"Worth it." 
 
Bruce actually laughed. 
 
Just once. 
 
Short. 
 
Dry. 
 
Real. 
 
Joker's eyes widened. 
 
Joker: "There he is." 
 
"I was beginning to think I'd imagined him." 
 
Bruce looked toward the river. 
 
Bruce: "You remember the giant penny?" 
 
Joker groaned dramatically. 
 
Joker: "You hit me with it." 
 
Bruce: "You tried to drop it on City Hall." 
 
Joker: "Details." 
 
Bruce: "You complained the whole ambulance ride." 
 
Joker pointed a finger. 
 
Joker: "It was heavy." 
 
Bruce nodded. 
 
Bruce: "It was." 
 
Joker smiled. 
 
Joker: "And the dinosaur?" 
 
Bruce sighed. 
 
Bruce: "You stole a dinosaur." 
 
Joker: "I borrowed it." 
 
Bruce: "You painted it purple." 
 
Joker: "It looked better." 
 
Bruce shook his head. 
 
Bruce: "It absolutely did not." 
 
The two old enemies laughed together. 
 
The sound disappeared into the rain. 
 
Neither noticed how strange that would have seemed years ago. 
 
Headlights appeared behind them. 
 
A black sedan rolled quietly onto the pier. 
 
A young man stepped out holding an umbrella. 
 
He approached respectfully. 
 
Butler: "Mr. Wayne." 
 
"The rain's getting heavier." 
 
"We should head home." 
 
Bruce nodded. 
 
Bruce: "Alright." 
 
The butler hesitated. 
 
He looked toward the empty stretch of railing beside Bruce. 
 
As if sensing someone had been there. 
 
Then quietly returned to the car. 
 
Bruce took one last look across the river. 
 
Bruce: "I suppose..." 
 
"...this is goodbye." 
 
No answer. 
 
Bruce turned. 
 
The space beside him was empty. 
 
The Joker was gone. 
 
No footsteps. 
 
No laughter. 
 
No boat. 
 
No impossible escape in sight. 
 
Only a single playing card resting on the wet railing. 
 
Bruce picked it up. 
 
A Joker. 
 
On the back... 
 
Written in faded green ink. 
 
**Till next time, Bats.** 
 
Bruce stared at it for a long while. 
 
Then he smiled. 
 
Not because he expected another meeting. 
 
Not because he believed the Joker was still hiding nearby. 
 
But because... 
 
After a lifetime of trying to defeat one another... 
 
Neither of them had ever really wanted the story to end. 
 
Bruce slipped the card into the inside pocket of his coat. 
 
Right beside an old photograph. 
 
One with a butler. 
 
Four Robins. 
 
A woman dressed like a cat. 
 
And a man in a cape... 
 
Who, for one brief evening on a rain-soaked pier, had simply been Bruce. 
 
The sedan door closed softly. 
 
The car disappeared into the Gotham night. 
 
Behind them, the river kept flowing. 
 
As it always had. 
 
As it always would. 
 
And somewhere, carried by the rain, there was the faintest echo of a laugh. 
 
This time... 
 
Bruce didn't turn around.
